Think of a helper function like a recipe card in a cookbook. The head chef — your `main` function — does not need to know every detail of how a sauce is made. They simply call out "make the sauce," and a specialist handles it. Crucially, though, the kitchen staff must be told that the sauce specialist *exists* before service begins, even if the full recipe is posted on the wall later.

In C and C++, the compiler reads your file strictly from top to bottom. If `main` tries to call a helper that has not been introduced yet, the compiler will abort — it simply does not know what that helper is.

The solution is a **function prototype**: a single-line declaration placed above `main` that announces the helper's name, its return type, and its parameters. The full definition of the helper can then appear further down in the file. [1](https://cs50.harvard.edu/x/2025/notes/2/)

You’re allocating resources for a ﬁle handle (stored in a FILE pointer), 
which you must then 
#include <stdio.h>

// do stuff; then close and free resources 
fclose( output ); 
return 0; 
} 
Every time you malloc, you must remember to free the memory when 
you are done! C does not do this for you and it will otherwise result in a 
resource leak. 
Andre Kessler

In IEEE 754, the distinction is made entirely by the **raw exponent field** — the 8 bits that represent `e` in the formula:

> x = (−1)^sign · (1.m₂₂m₂₁...m₀) · 2^(e − bias)

The rule is precise and binary:

| Exponent field value | Classification | Implied leading bit |
|---|---|---|
| `00000000` (all zeros) | **Denormalized** | `0.` |
| `00000001` through `11111110` | **Normalized** | `1.` |
| `11111111` (all ones) | `NaN` / `Inf` | — |

So the test is simply: if the raw 8-bit exponent field equals **zero**, the number is denormalized and the mantissa is interpreted as `0.m₂₂m₂₁...m₀`. Otherwise, it is normalized and the mantissa is interpreted as `1.m₂₂m₂₁...m₀`. [1](ass1_p1.pdf)

Notice that this means the sign bit plays **no role** in this determination — which is exactly what we established in your previous turn.

Now, given that you can extract the exponent field using bitwise operations on your `union float_bits`, what single comparison would let you decide which prefix to print?

Think of a vending machine. When you walk up to it, you do not hand it anything — you just press a button and it does its job. The machine takes **no input from you** to start up; it simply runs.

In C, `main(void)` works the same way. The word `void` inside the parentheses is your way of telling the compiler: "this function takes **no arguments** — nothing needs to be handed to it for it to start running."

```c
int main(void)  // "Start here, and expect nothing handed in"
{
    printf("hello, world\n");
}
```

The `int` at the front is a separate idea — it describes what `main` *gives back* to the operating system when it finishes, which you will explore soon.

So here is a question to check your understanding: if `void` in the parentheses means "takes nothing in," what do you think it might mean when you see `void` *before* a function's name — like `void meow(void)`? [1](https://cs50.harvard.edu/x/2025/notes/1/)

Think of writing a recipe versus actually cooking the meal. Writing the recipe down does not produce any food — you still have to take it to the kitchen and cook it.

In C, `code hello.c` is like **writing the recipe**. It simply opens your file in the editor so you can type your instructions. It does not compile or run anything.

To actually produce output, you need two more steps after you have saved your file:

```
make hello
./hello
```

`make hello` is the **compiler** — it reads your C source code and turns it into an executable program. `./hello` is what actually **runs** that program and produces output in the terminal. [1](https://cs50.harvard.edu/x/2025/notes/1/)

So here is a guiding question: after you run `make hello`, what do you think would happen if you skipped `./hello` and just typed `make hello` again?

sign

Content: [P: Philosophy] Rule P.5: P.5: Prefer compile-time checking to run-time checking
Example: // Int is an alias used for integers
int bits = 0; // don't: avoidable code
for (Int i = 1; i; i <<= 1)
 ++bits;
if (bits < 32)
 cerr << "Int too small\n";
This example fails to achieve what it is trying to achieve (because overflow is undefined) and should be replaced with a simple 
static_assert
:
// Int is an alias used for integers
static_assert(sizeof(Int) >= 4); // do: compile-time check
Or better still just use the type system and replace 
Int
 with 
int32_t
.
```cpp
// Int is an alias used for integers
int bits = 0;         // don't: avoidable code
for (Int i = 1; i; i <<= 1)
    ++bits;
if (bits < 32)
    cerr << "Int too small\n";

// Int is an alias used for integers
static_assert(sizeof(Int) >= 4);    // do: compile-time check
```

The three key member functions you will need are:

- **`notify_one()`** — wakes up one waiting thread
- **`notify_all()`** — wakes up all waiting threads

```
Bit: 31 | 30 -------- 23 | 22 --------------- 0
```

A **right shift** (`>>`) moves bits toward position 0. A **mask** (`&`) zeroes out bits you do not want, using a pattern like `0xFF` (which is `00000000 11111111` in binary — it keeps only the lowest 8 bits).

So for a generic 8-bit field sitting at bits 30–23, the pattern is always: shift it down to position 0, then mask off anything above it.

A **shift** (`>>`) slides all bits right. A **mask** (`&`) keeps only the bits you want:

```
bits = 0b 1 01111100 00000000000000000000000

                                    ^^^^^^^^^
                 now the 8 exponent bits are at the bottom

(bits >> 23) & 0xFF  -->  keeps ONLY those bottom 8 bits
```

[Syllabus]
Content: MIT 2014 — Week 1
Course Meeting Times
Lectures: 3 sessions / week; 2 hrs / session
Open Labs: 1 session / week; 2 hrs / session
Course Description
Do you want to learn how create blazing fast programs, be organized about developing a software project, write C/C++ code that will keep the people who maintain it very happy, learn how to ace an interview in either of these languages since you’ll know them so well, and understand how to properly debug your code when you inevitably run into problems? Then this might be the crash course for you.
This course is a fast-paced introduction to the C and C++ programming languages, both of which are useful for classes, research, and jobs. Focus will be placed on practical knowledge, especially best practices, the powerful advantages C/C++ can offer, and modern features of C++. Students will come away with an understanding of when and why you might want to use C/C++ over another language, how both “low-level” and more abstracted programming can help you, and how to best develop your own software projects in these languages. [DIRECT_THEORY_SCAFFOLD]

A range-based for loop in C++ works over any type that exposes a **begin** and **end** iterator — this includes raw arrays, `std::string`, and all standard containers [1](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/algorithm/ranges/for_each).

For a `char` array or `std::string`, the loop variable takes on each character value in sequence:

```cpp
const std::string VALID_GRADES = "ABCDF";
for (char c : VALID_GRADES) {
    // c is 'A', then 'B', then 'C', then 'D', then 'F'
}
```

The key formal rule is this: the compiler internally rewrites the range-based for loop as a traditional iterator loop, calling `begin()` and `end()` on the range. For a raw C-style `char` array, the compiler knows its size at compile time and can generate those bounds automatically.

The critical distinction from a traditional `for` loop is that you never manage an index variable — you declare what **type** you want to receive on each iteration, and the compiler handles the traversal.

Given that, here is a question to deepen your understanding: if you declared your loop variable as `char& c` instead of `char c`, what would be fundamentally different about how `c` relates to the original string?

That is exactly the right instinct. The C++ mechanism for enforcing read-only access on a reference is the `const` qualifier.

Formally, a `const` reference binds to an object but prohibits any modification through that binding. The compiler will produce a hard error if you attempt to write to it [1](https://isocpp.github.io/CppCoreGuidelines/CppCoreGuidelines#con1-by-default-make-objects-immutable):

```cpp
for (const char& c : VALID_GRADES) {
    // reading c is fine
    // c = 'X'; would be a compile-time error
}
```

The C++ Core Guidelines state a clear principle here: **make objects immutable by default**, and only relax that constraint when mutation is explicitly required. This applies equally to loop variables.

For a `char` specifically, the practical recommendation is actually `const char` (by value) rather than `const char&`, since copying a single byte is no more expensive than an indirection. However, the `const char&` form is semantically correct and becomes the preferred pattern when the element type is large.

Now, connecting this back to your earlier reasoning: you identified that you are only reading, which means `const` is the right constraint. What do you think would happen at **compile time** if you accidentally wrote `c = grade;` inside a loop declared with `const char& c`?

Yes, that is exactly right — using `char& c` avoids a copy and instead gives you a direct alias to each character in the original string.

Formally, the C++ Core Guidelines state that for types that are cheap to copy — such as `char`, `int`, or a pointer — passing or binding by value is often **equally fast or faster** than by reference, because a reference still requires an indirection to access the underlying memory [1](https://isocpp.github.io/CppCoreGuidelines/CppCoreGuidelines#f16-for-in-parameters-pass-cheaply-copied-types-by-value-and-others-by-reference-to-const).

So for a `char`, the practical performance difference is negligible. The more important semantic distinction is this: `char& c` is an **alias** — if you wrote to `c`, you would be modifying the original string. `char c` is a **copy** — writing to it leaves the original untouched.

Given that, here is the deeper question to consider: in your grade-validation loop, are you ever intending to **modify** the characters in `VALID_GRADES`, or are you only **reading** them?

Content: [F: Functions]
Rule F.16: F.16: For “in” parameters, pass cheaply-copied types by value and others by reference to const
Reason: Both let the caller know that a function will not modify the argument, and both allow initialization by rvalues.

size_t binary_search( int *data, size_t N, int value ) { 
size_t lo = 0, hi = N - 1; 
while( lo < hi ) { 
size_t mid = lo + ( hi - lo ) / 2; 
if( data[mid] < value ) { 
lo = mid + 1; 
} else { 
hi = mid; 
} 
} 
return ( hi == lo && data[lo] == value ) ? lo : N; 
}

Think about a sticky note. You write a quick instruction on it — "add 5 to whatever number you get" — hand it to someone, and they use it once and throw it away. You never gave that instruction a formal name, filed it anywhere, or defined it as a permanent procedure. It was just a small, self-contained action defined exactly where it was needed.

A C++ lambda is the programming equivalent of that sticky note. It is an anonymous function — defined inline, at the point of use, without a name.

Here is the minimal anatomy of a lambda:

```cpp
auto add5 = [](int x) { return x + 5; };
```

The `[]` is called the **capture clause**, the `(int x)` is the parameter list, and the body works exactly like any other function body.

You are on the right track about parameters, but there is actually more to that `[]` capture clause than it first appears. Think back to the sticky note analogy — what if, when you wrote that note, you could also staple a copy of some information from your desk onto it? The person using the note would then have that surrounding context without you explicitly passing it as a parameter every time.

That is precisely what the capture clause controls. It does not have to be empty. You can instruct the lambda to **capture** variables from its enclosing scope — either by value or by reference — making them available inside the lambda body just as naturally as any local variable [1](Lecture6.pdf).

So the distinction you are drawing — "small operation with parameters" versus "complex operation needing a full class" — is actually a spectrum, not a binary. The capture clause is what sits in the middle of that spectrum.

With that in mind, revisit your earlier reasoning: if a lambda can capture variables from its surrounding scope, does the limitation you identified still hold?

The standard pattern for `std::condition_variable::wait()` requires that the consumer already holds the lock **before** calling `wait()`. The reason is subtle but important: `wait()` must **atomically** release the lock and suspend the thread. If the unlock and the sleep were two separate steps, the producer could sneak in and call `notify_one()` in between — and the consumer would sleep forever, missing the notification entirely. This is called a **spurious wakeup / lost wakeup** race.

The idiomatic C++ solution is `std::unique_lock` (not `std::lock_guard`), because `wait()` requires a lock it can release and re-acquire internally.

So the corrected consumer sequence is:

1. Acquire `std::unique_lock`
2. Call `cv.wait(lock, predicate)` — this atomically releases the lock and blocks
3. On notification, the lock is **automatically re-acquired** before your thread resumes
4. Walk the cart, collect totals
5. Release the lock, then print

**[ANALOGY_SCAFFOLD]**

Think of a condition variable like a waiting room at a doctor's office. A patient (thread) enters the waiting room only after checking in at the front desk — that is, after acquiring a lock. When the nurse calls them (the condition variable is notified), the patient must re-check with the front desk before proceeding into the exam room.

The critical detail is this: while the patient is sitting and waiting, they must be able to **temporarily release** their hold on the front desk so other patients can check in. This is exactly what `std::unique_lock` enables that `std::lock_guard` does not — it supports being unlocked and re-locked mid-scope. A condition variable's `wait()` call requires this ability to atomically release the lock during the wait and reacquire it upon waking.

This is why `std::condition_variable` in the C++ standard library is designed to work specifically with `std::unique_lock<std::mutex>`.

Your reasoning about global variables is exactly right, and it shows you have a solid grasp of why the capture list is empty in that case.

Here is an analogy to anchor the next step. Think of a lambda as a small, self-contained errand runner you dispatch from your kitchen. If the ingredient it needs is already in the pantry (a global variable), it can walk in and grab it any time — no preparation needed. But if the ingredient is sitting on *your* counter (a local variable in the enclosing function), you have to physically hand it to the errand runner before you send it off, or it will have no idea the ingredient exists.

That "handing off" is precisely what the capture list `[...]` is for.

When `ready` is a local variable, the lambda's body has no automatic access to the enclosing scope. You must explicitly declare how to bring it in. C++ gives you two fundamental choices:

- `[ready]` — capture **by value** (the lambda gets its own copy at the moment of creation)
- `[&ready]` — capture **by reference** (the lambda holds a reference to the original variable)

For a condition variable predicate, which of these two do you think would be the correct choice, and why?

[1](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/language/lambda)

That is precisely the right conclusion, and it is one of the most important safety rules in C++ regarding reference captures.

The formal term for what you have described is a **dangling reference**. The C++ standard is explicit on this: when a lambda captures a local variable by reference, the lambda does not extend the lifetime of that variable in any way. If the variable is destroyed — because it goes out of scope, or because the owning object is deallocated — the lambda is left holding a reference to memory that is no longer valid. Any subsequent access through that reference is **undefined behavior**. [1](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/language/lambda)

In the context of `cv.wait()`, this is especially dangerous because the wait may outlive the stack frame where `ready` was declared. The standard pattern to avoid this is to ensure `ready` (and the mutex, and the condition variable itself) all share the same lifetime — typically by making them members of a shared object, or as you originally observed, by making them globals with static storage duration, which live for the entire program.

This is actually one of the motivating reasons why `std::unique_ptr` and shared ownership patterns (covered in your Week 6 material) exist: to give the programmer precise, explicit control over object lifetimes rather than relying on stack scope alone.

Does this lifetime constraint change how you would design a class that wraps a condition variable and its associated predicate state?

Content: [P: Philosophy] Rule P.5: P.5: Prefer compile-time checking to run-time checking
Example: // Int is an alias used for integers
int bits = 0; // don't: avoidable code
for (Int i = 1; i; i <<= 1)
 ++bits;
if (bits < 32)
 cerr << "Int too small\n";
This example fails to achieve what it is trying to achieve (because overflow is undefined) and should be replaced with a simple 
static_assert
:
// Int is an alias used for integers
static_assert(sizeof(Int) >= 4); // do: compile-time check
Or better still just use the type system and replace 
Int
 with 
int32_t
.
```cpp
// Int is an alias used for integers
int bits = 0;         // don't: avoidable code
for (Int i = 1; i; i <<= 1)
    ++bits;
if (bits < 32)
    cerr << "Int too small\n";

// Int is an alias used for integers
static_assert(sizeof(Int) >= 4);    // do: compile-time check
```

Example, bad: vector<int> vec = /*...*/;

for (int i = 0; i < vec.size(); i += 2) // might not be big enough
 cout << vec[i] << '\n';
for (unsigned i = 0; i < vec.size(); i += 2) // risk wraparound
 cout << vec[i] << '\n';
for (auto i = 0; i < vec.size(); i += 2) // might not be big enough
 cout << vec[i] << '\n';
for (vector<int>::size_type i = 0; i < vec.size(); i += 2) // verbose
 cout << vec[i] << '\n';
for (auto i = vec.size()-1; i >= 0; i -= 2) // bug
 cout << vec[i] << '\n';
for (int i = vec.size()-1; i >= 0; i -= 2) // might not be big enough
 cout << vec[i] << '\n';
